cards.headline: Byron Donalds holds Martin County roundtable on insurance costs, property taxes
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds met with Martin County residents Wednesday for a roundtable discussion on affordability issues including homeowners insurance and p
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds met with Martin County residents Wednesday for a roundtable discussion on affordability issues including homeowners insurance and property taxes. The event at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart drew about a dozen voters including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners.

 Donalds fielded questions for about an hour in a small meeting room, encouraging open dialogue rather than delivering a formal speech. One homeowner asked what could be done about rising insurance costs, saying the increases are pricing people out of their homes. Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes.

 When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. Donalds said healthcare reforms should address in-network and out-of-network issues and prior authorizations.

 In an interview afterward, Donalds addressed recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. Donalds said the campaign is not distancing itself from Trump and that website changes had been planned for about two months following the primary. Donalds said the campaign wanted the website to focus purely on the issues.

 Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election, which is six weeks away.

cards.headline: Donalds backs Amendment 3 homestead exemption; Jolly opposes, debate off the table
cards.teaser: Republican Byron Donalds supports Amendment 3's expansion of Florida's homestead tax exemption to $250,000, while Democrat David Jolly opposes the measure and confirmed his decision not to debate Donalds before the November election.
cards.body:
Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly presented opposing positions Wednesday on Amendment 3, the ballot measure that would raise Florida's homestead tax exemption to $250,000 over two years, during the WLRN Sunshine Economy Summit in downtown Fort Lauderdale.

 Donalds told the audience he supports the measure. "I think voters need relief. I think the property owners need relief," Donalds said.

 Jolly said he anticipates voting against Amendment 3. "I don't think the math works, and I think we know that because even Ron DeSantis now won't campaign for Amendment 3, and our sheriffs have come out and said, 'Please don't do this. It's going to defund services,'" Jolly said. The two gubernatorial nominees spoke in back-to-back 30-minute panel discussions but were kept separate throughout the event.

 The candidates also clashed on hurricane insurance reform. Jolly proposed a sovereign wealth fund that would absorb hurricane and wind insurance burdens for Floridians. "We are not going to solve this without government taking on a larger role in backing this.

 Otherwise, people are going to be priced out of their homes," Jolly said. Donalds said that plan won't work and instead called for eliminating a premium surcharge that contributes to the state's catastrophic fund. "We get through this hurricane season, the Cat Fund is estimated to have somewhere between 13 and 13-and-a-half billion dollars.

 So why do we have a 25% kicker on top to keep filling the Cat Fund, whose statutory limit is $17 billion? My view is to get rid of the kicker. That would lower premiums for every policyholder in the state," Donalds said.

 Jolly confirmed earlier this week he will not debate Donalds, making this the first gubernatorial election in 50 years in which Florida voters won't see the nominees face off. "It just became obvious that this is not going to contribute to a more constructive political environment, and that's the bottom line. I understand some people have concerns about it.

 I just promise you, for me, this is a moment bigger than politics," Jolly told reporters after his panel discussion. Donalds said he wants the debate to happen. "He said something about how I lied about him — which is a lie, by the way — and so he doesn't want to debate.

 Well, that's what debates are for: to clarify all that stuff. The ball's in his court," Donalds said. When asked if his decision could change, Jolly said his decision is final. Both candidates share a commitment to keeping Florida free of a state income tax.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie HOA offers bulk tree program as Sept. 30 deadline nears in Cadence at Tradition dispute
cards.teaser: The Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association is offering residents a chance to join its bulk tree-purchase program as the Sept. 30 deadline approaches for replacing dead trees, even as homeowners continue to dispute responsibility for trees on swales.
cards.body:
The Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association is offering residents a chance to participate in its bulk tree-purchase program as the Sept. 30 deadline approaches for replacing dead trees in the community. Homeowners in the Port St. Lucie community received notices dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc. demanding dead trees on their property be replaced by Sept. 30 or face escalation, but many residents say the trees are on swales and should be the HOA's responsibility.

 A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA said the association is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. The firm said residents are responsible for replacing trees in limited common areas such as rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons.

 Because the HOA is purchasing and installing trees in bulk, it has invited residents to participate in the program. The program allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally, according to the statement.

 Homeowner Chip Collison said the dead trees were in common areas, not in yards, and he wants the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. Keyla Peguero, another homeowner at Cadence at Tradition, said she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it. She said she is not willing to do it again and should not have had to do it in the first place.

 The HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees at the homeowners' expense. Some residents say new trees should be planted in April at the start of the growing season rather than now. Collison said if new trees are planted now during hurricane season, a strong hurricane could destroy them and they would have to be redone again. The Sept. 1 notice from Campbell Property Management does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees by the deadline.

 Jolly confirmed earlier this week he will not debate Donalds, making this the first gubernatorial election in 50 years in which Florida voters won't see the nominees face off. "It just became obvious that this is not going to contribute to a more constructive political environment, and that's the bottom line. I understand some people have concerns about it.

 I just promise you, for me, this is a moment bigger than politics," Jolly told reporters after his panel discussion. Donalds said he wants the debate to happen. "He said something about how I lied about him — which is a lie, by the way — and so he doesn't want to debate.

 Well, that's what debates are for: to clarify all that stuff. The ball's in his court," Donalds said. When asked if his decision could change, Jolly said his decision is final. Both candidates share a commitment to keeping Florida free of a state income tax.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie HOA offers bulk tree program as Sept. 30 deadline nears in Cadence at Tradition dispute
cards.teaser: The Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association is offering residents a chance to join its bulk tree-purchase program as the Sept. 30 deadline approaches for replacing dead trees, even as homeowners continue to dispute responsibility for trees on swales.
cards.body:
The Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association is offering residents a chance to participate in its bulk tree-purchase program as the Sept. 30 deadline approaches for replacing dead trees in the community. Homeowners in the Port St. Lucie community received notices dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc. demanding dead trees on their property be replaced by Sept. 30 or face escalation, but many residents say the trees are on swales and should be the HOA's responsibility.

 A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA said the association is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. The firm said residents are responsible for replacing trees in limited common areas such as rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons.

 Because the HOA is purchasing and installing trees in bulk, it has invited residents to participate in the program. The program allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally, according to the statement.

 Homeowner Chip Collison said the dead trees were in common areas, not in yards, and he wants the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. Keyla Peguero, another homeowner at Cadence at Tradition, said she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it. She said she is not willing to do it again and should not have had to do it in the first place.

 The HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees at the homeowners' expense. Some residents say new trees should be planted in April at the start of the growing season rather than now. Collison said if new trees are planted now during hurricane season, a strong hurricane could destroy them and they would have to be redone again. The Sept. 1 notice from Campbell Property Management does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees by the deadline.
